html:
The Library of Ashurbanipal was a royal collection of tens of thousands of clay tablets gathered at Nineveh, in northern Iraq, by Ashurbanipal, the last great king of Assyria, who ruled from 668 to about 631 BCE.

Ashurbanipal, who boasted that he could read, had scribes copy texts from across Mesopotamia: omens, spells, medicine, word lists, and literature. When Nineveh was sacked in 612 BCE, the palaces burned, which baked the tablets hard.

British diggers found them in the 1850s, and they went to the British Museum. In 1872 George Smith read in them a flood story much like Noah's, part of the Epic of Gilgamesh, which caused a sensation. Much of what we know of cuneiform literature comes from this library.
sum: The Library of Ashurbanipal was a royal collection of tens of thousands of clay tablets gathered at Nineveh, in northern Iraq, by Ashurbanipal, the last great king of Assyria, who ruled from 668 to about 631 BCE.
